findings.quote: Friction that does not let the surfaces slip, as under a ball rolling without slipping, does zero work.
findings.problem: New in the round-3 fix. Stated as a general rule, but static friction does work on an object whenever the object moves while the surface carries it. A box carried up a sloped conveyor belt at steady speed does not slip, yet static friction points along its displacement and does positive work that raises its $PE$. A crate on the bed of a speeding-up truck gains $KE$ only through static friction. By the lesson's own $W=Fd\cos\theta$, a nonzero force along a nonzero displacement does nonzero work. The rule holds only when the surface is at rest, as for the rolling ball; the lesson attaches that limit to sliding friction ("a surface at rest") but not here. A student who applies it to a conveyor or truck item says friction does no work and gets the energy accounting wrong.
findings.source: Checklist B01; the lesson's own formula $W=Fd\cos\theta$ applied in the ground frame; OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 7.1 Work (work depends on the displacement of the point of application); reader rules, Added after the Sol audit

findings.quote: If only conservative forces do work, mechanical energy stays the same:
findings.problem: The lesson defines $PE$ only as gravitational potential energy, $mgh$, and defines mechanical energy as $KE+PE$. A spring force is conservative, so by this sentence a block pushed from rest along level, frictionless ground by a spring keeps $KE+PE$ constant. In fact its $KE$ rises while $mgh$ does not change, so $KE+mgh$ rises, and $W_{nc}=\Delta(KE+PE)$ gives $0$ equal to a positive number. The statement is true only if mechanical energy also counts the energy a spring stores, which the lesson never says. The round-3 L25 finding (spring in the shortcut) was fixed by removing the spring from Speed Tricks, but this Core Concept sentence keeps the same gap in general form.
findings.source: Checklist B01; OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 8.1 Potential Energy of a System and 8.3 Conservation of Energy (mechanical energy includes elastic potential energy); round-3 read, L25 finding

findings.quote: A freely falling object, with air ignored, gains about $9.8\ \text{m/s}$ of speed every second.
findings.problem: Fails for a known case. The kinematics lesson defines free fall as motion with only gravity acting and says it includes an object going up after a throw. That object loses about $9.8\ \text{m/s}$ of speed each second while it rises. A ball thrown sideways is also in free fall, and its speed grows by less than $9.8\ \text{m/s}$ in the first second, since only the vertical part of its velocity changes by that amount. What $g$ fixes is the change in velocity, $9.8\ \text{m/s}$ downward each second, not the gain in speed. The sentence holds only for an object dropped or thrown straight down.
findings.source: Checklist B01; content/lessons/science/physics/kinematics.md, Free Fall ("This includes an object going up after a throw"); OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 3.5 Free Fall; reader rules, Added after the Sol audit

findings.quote: The total energy of an isolated system stays constant.
findings.problem: The lesson's goal is to tell mechanical energy conservation apart from total energy conservation, and this sentence carries the condition for total energy conservation. The term "isolated system" (the objects under study, with no energy entering or leaving from outside) is never explained, and no prerequisite lesson is named for it. A Grade 5 reader cannot tell when total energy stays constant, for example why a block pushed by a motor gains energy without breaking the law.
findings.source: Checklist L25; LSG Teaching completeness; brief goal (distinguish mechanical energy conservation from total energy conservation)

findings.quote: the speed is steady, so the net force is zero
findings.problem: Example #8(b) rests on Newton's first law (steady speed in a straight line means zero net force) to set the crane's force equal to the weight. Example #4 also relies on "net force" ("The push is the net force, along the motion."). The lesson defines net work but never explains net force or the first law, and names no prerequisite lesson for them, while it does name one for effort and load. A student without the dynamics lesson cannot see why $F=mg$ in this step.
findings.source: Checklist L25; LSG Teaching completeness; reader rules, Added after the Sol audit (list every term an example uses and confirm it is taught or its prerequisite named)
